display_name: Parallax Feedback 360 plate gripper (rack and pinion, CAN)
status_note: The COMMAND model is now real - taken from Gripper/API.md and Gripper/klipper/gripper_macros.cfg in the SDL_Gcode repo, 2026-10-06. What is still missing is GEOMETRY: every z_for_labware value is null, so a protocol that moves the gripper to a plate refuses until they are measured. The previous version of this file modelled the gripper as POSITIONAL (open_pos / closed_pos / grip_pos) and that was simply wrong for this hardware - see no_position below.

no_position.note: THE SERVO HAS NO POSITION. The Parallax Feedback 360's feedback output has failed on two units, so the firmware runs OPEN LOOP and every motion is TIMED, not positional. There is no 'open to 30 degrees', only 'open for 400 ms'. Any position field in a reply reads n/a. This is a hardware fault, not a software choice. Do not reintroduce a *_pos field: a number that cannot be measured or commanded is worse than an absent one.

actuator.open_ms_max_note: FIRMWARE CLAMP, and the single most dangerous number in this file. Closing ends at a hard stop; opening ends at NOTHING. Past full travel the racks disengage from the pinion and the mechanism must be reassembled by hand. There is no software recovery. Machine.gripper_open refuses anything above this rather than letting the firmware silently clamp, so the gcode says what was asked for. 765 since 2026-10-16, matching OPEN_LIMIT_MS in the firmware (SDL_Gcode Gripper/board/boardpins.py). The history there: 1200 -> 950 -> 850 -> 765 against a measured 1000 ms disengagement point, and '850 still ran slightly long and the jaws came off the racks'. This file still said 850, so the library would have passed an open the firmware had already found unsafe - and the firmware's silent clamp would have hidden it.
actuator.grip_ma_note: 500 is the firmware clamp; the hardware ceiling is about 570 mA. A setpoint above the clamp is SILENTLY reduced by the firmware, which is why the library refuses it instead. --ma is repeatable but UNCALIBRATED against force: it is not newtons.

hold.note: A grip is a CONTROLLED STALL, not a clamp - this servo has no holding torque at rest. Full commanded current for the first 20 s, reduced for the next 120, then de-energised with a fault raised. Design every sequence to put the part down before 140 s. If a plate must be held longer, this actuator is the wrong tool and the fixture needs a mechanical detent.
hold.duty_note: HOLD_DUTY_MAX_MS of energised hold is permitted in any HOLD_DUTY_WINDOW_MS (boardpins.py: 150 s in 300 s). Past it the board raises FLT_HOLD_EXPIRED and de-energises - with a plate in the jaws, if the timing is unlucky. A repeated-grip program has to pace itself against this; gripper_offset_trials.py inserts cooldown dwells at slice time.

requires_home_note: OPEN, CLOSE and GRIP are refused by the firmware until HOME has run. Home drives into the closed stop and calls that zero. It costs about a second and re-establishes the only reference the timed model has, so when in doubt, home. Home again after any ST_LIMIT, ST_ABORTED or power cycle.

macros.note: From Gripper/klipper/gripper_macros.cfg, which must be included from printer.cfg and needs the gcode_shell_command extra. GRIPPER_IMU is an ADDITION - the shipped cfg had no IMU macro, so there was no way to ask for a measurement from gcode at all. GRIPPER_MACROS_VERSION prints which copy of the cfg Klipper loaded: the installed copy sits next to printer.cfg and drifted from the repo once already, keeping an obsolete 'needs CSV=' guard after CSV had become optional. Symlink the cfg rather than copying it. GRIPPER_TRIAL* front host/trial_session.py, which runs offset_trials.py's procedure one step per macro and writes its two files, <stem>_plate.csv and <stem>_pcb.csv. trial_home REFUSES while the board reports holding, trial_grip records the board's reply as grip_status, and trial_burst skips the raised and lowered captures of a refused grip - the three places a G-code program, which cannot branch, would otherwise differ from the script.
macros.do_not_use_note: DANGEROUS ON THIS MACHINE. Both do relative Z moves with the sign convention of a normal printer - GRIPPER_PICK emits G1 Z+40 and calls it a lift. Here +Z is DOWN, so that command drives the gripper 40 mm INTO the plate. This library emits absolute Z through Machine, which knows the convention.

imu_storage.note: Captures are written to capture_dir on the Pi's LOCAL disk and copied to dest_dir when the capture stops. Never recorded straight onto the share: a 100 Hz capture writing to a mount that stalls or drops takes the run with it, and it would surface as a short CSV rather than an error. Copy-after means a share that is down costs the copy, not the data. The macro layer owns both paths now: _GRIPPER_IMU_CFG in gripper_macros.cfg holds local_dir and nas_dir, and GRIPPER_IMU_START passes --csv and --dest explicitly rather than letting imu_session's own defaults apply. A protocol that sends no csv_dir/dest_dir therefore still lands here, and the macro echoes both paths before the capture starts - the run that could not be found on 2026-10-06 said neither. The per-sensor files are intermediates named <stem>.pcb.part.csv and <stem>.plate.part.csv; stop merges and deletes them, and keeps them if the merge fails, so anything left with '.part.' in the name is a capture that did not finish.
imu_storage.mount_note: dest_dir is a path ON THE PI and the share must already be mounted there. Confirmed by the operator 2026-10-06: it is mounted at /mnt/nas, so UNC \\ICE-NAS\Data\GC_ARCCS\GripperIMU is /mnt/nas/GC_ARCCS/GripperIMU here. MIND THE SEPARATOR - the operator wrote it as \mnt\nas\..., which is how Windows renders a path, but the capture runs on Linux and backslashes are not separators there. Passed through, \mnt\nas\GC_ARCCS\GripperIMU would be ONE filename containing backslashes, and the data would be written successfully somewhere nobody looks - which is why Machine.gripper_imu_start refuses any destination containing one. If the share moves, pass --dest-dir with forward slashes; nothing on the slicing machine can check a mount on the Pi.
imu_storage.one_file: A capture produces ONE csv - <label>_<YYYYmmdd_HHMMSS>.csv - holding both IMUs and every mark. Long format: one row per sample, with a `source` column of pcb (board IMU over CAN), plate (the Pi's I2C IMU on the plate carrier) or mark (a labelled instant, `label` says which). It is NOT wide - the two sensors free-run at slightly different rates with no shared trigger, so one row per instant would mean resampling, and an interpolated row is an invented measurement that reads exactly like a recorded one. Pivot afterwards if you want it wide. The join key is wall_clock, the Pi's epoch clock and the only clock both share; t_s is recomputed as seconds from the first sample. A pcb row's wall_clock is stamped on ARRIVAL at the Pi, not at sampling, so it carries CAN latency - fine for comparing the timing of an event across the two sensors, not for absolute phase to better than a few ms. A RUN is one program's worth of captures appending to one CSV: GRIPPER_IMU_RUN_BEGIN opens it, every capture appends, GRIPPER_IMU_RUN_END closes it and copies it. The board IMU cannot be commanded while it streams, so a multi-cycle run is several captures whatever happens - the run file is what still makes it one CSV. The `capture` column names which one a row came from, and t_s restarts within each; wall_clock orders the whole run. The Pi applies the timestamp, not the slicer: a slicer-stamped name would change the generated gcode on every slice.
imu_storage.rate_note: Both sensors sample at this rate unless a capture overrides it. One rate for both is the point: before 2026-10-06 an omitted rate meant the board ran at gripctl's default and the plate logger at 100 Hz, so one file held two streams at different rates with only the `source` column distinguishing them. 50 Hz is chosen for orientation work.

shell_command.note: Whether RUN_SHELL_COMMAND blocks until the process exits is INSTALL-DEPENDENT and has not been tested here. While blocks is null the library emits a G4 guard dwell after every gripper macro, so a following move cannot start while the gripper is still running. Test it once, set blocks true, and the dwells disappear - that is about 3.5 s a cycle.
shell_command.unguarded_note: These write a context file and touch neither the gantry nor the board, so a following move cannot collide with them whether or not the shell command blocks. Without a guard, a non-blocking install would at worst stamp a phase change a few hundred ms late. imu_mark is NOT here: a mark still running when imu_stop merges is a lost mark.
shell_command.busy_note: trial_burst holds the host for its settle plus its samples, and the board reads no command queue while it streams. Its guard is guard_dwell_ms PLUS that busy time, so a following GRIPPER_* command is not queued behind it.

gripper_pick_9.note: Operator-measured 2026-10-06. +Z is DOWN, so: approach 90 is the height the gripper arrives and leaves at; it descends to 107 to close on the part; it releases at 100. RELEASE IS 7 mm ABOVE THE GRIP, so the part falls 7 mm when it is let go. That is deliberate and the protocol declares the drop explicitly - Machine.release refuses any drop it was not told to expect, because releasing at height is the first rule in the gripper's API.

sbs_96_wellplate.note: UNMEASURED - this is what blocks a plate-handling protocol today. 'grip' is the commanded Z at which the jaws surround a seated plate; 'lift' is the Z to carry it at, which must be SMALLER (physically higher) than grip. Measure by jogging with the gripper fitted and open: lower until the jaws straddle the plate skirt, record that as grip; raise until the plate clears everything on the deck, record that as lift. Both are per-effector because the jaw reference sits at a different height from the p300 nosecone.

carries_labware_note: NOT TRACKED. Unlike a pipette, a gripper changes the deck LAYOUT at run time: picking a plate empties a slot and fills the effector. Machine.grip/release track whether something is held and at what Z it was picked, which is enough to enforce 'never release at height', but nothing moves the Placement in the Deck. A protocol that carries a plate to a different slot and dispenses into it there will compute the old coordinates. Transporting between slots needs that tracking first.

feedrates.note: The gripper has no feedrate of its own - the servo is timed, and gantry moves use the deck's.

todo_before_use: add GRIPPER_IMU to Gripper/klipper/gripper_macros.cfg (text is in docs/LAB.md)
test once whether RUN_SHELL_COMMAND blocks, then set shell_command.blocks
confirm the gripper never uses GRIPPER_PICK or GRIPPER_PLACE on this machine
teach Deck to move a Placement when a plate is carried between slots

capture_concurrency.note: Can a gripper command run while a capture is open? It depends which IMU is being captured. The BOARD IMU goes over CAN, so capturing it means CMD_IMU_READ, which gripnode runs as a blocking loop - unchanged as of 9d21235, and drain() still says the command queue is not read until the motion returns. So commands_during_capture stays false for any capture including _pcb. The PLATE IMU is a local I2C read on the Pi and touches the bus not at all, so a --plate-only capture CAN span a GRIPPER_GRIP or a GRIPPER_RELEASE. That is what plate_only_spans_commands records.
capture_concurrency.evidence: Gripper repo as of ae6c89f: the host side gained two IMUs (4840a0d), timestamps and a default NAS copy (ae73c8d), and a canonical instrumented cycle in API.md (ae6c89f). The BOARD side gained only boardpins OPEN_LIMIT_MS 950 -> 850 (9d21235). gripnode.imu_read() is still `for i in range(count)` with no dispatch of _pending, and gripctl.cmd_imu still issues ONE CMD_IMU_READ for the whole count rather than chunking it.
capture_concurrency.to_enable: Dispatch _pending inside imu_read()'s loop, guarded against a nested imu_read - see board/PROPOSAL_imu_concurrent.md. Flash it, confirm a grip issued mid-capture returns 'grip: done', then set this true. The protocol then emits the spanning sequence with no code change.
